To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
resistance to NRTI and minor PIs is transmitted in a pattern consistent with maternal viral load, while resistance to NNRTIs and major PIs are not transmitted.
the transmission of HIV-1 from mothers to their infants is not random, and the transmission of drug-resistant virus is not random.
the transmission of HIV-1 from mothers to infants was associated with resistance mutations to nucleoside and minor protease inhibitors but not to non-nucleosides or major protease inhibitors.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the transmission of drug resistance mutations from mother to infant and the impact this may have on the treatment of the infant.
the study of HIV resistance in viral isolations from mother-infant pairs.
the transmission of drug resistant HIV from infected mothers to their infants.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
transmission of NRTI-associated mutations is concordant with the predominant variant in the maternal virus, while transmission of NNRTI- or major PI-associated mutations is not.

the presence of resistance to NRTIs and minor PIs in the maternal isolate is a strong indicator for the presence of resistance in the infant, but that this is not true for NNRTI and major PI resistance.

the transmission of resistance mutations is dependent upon the nature of the mutation, the relative quantity of the mutant and wild-type virus, the drug to which it confers resistance, and the relative efficacy of the drug in the infant.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the presence of a mutation is necessary but not sufficient for the transmission of the resistance.
transmission of resistance mutations is not random but depends on the type and quantity of the mutation.
the presence of a resistance mutation in the maternal virus is not a good predictor of the presence of that mutation in the infant, except for mutations associated with NRTI and minor PI drugs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
resistance mutations associated with NRTI and minor PI drugs were concordant in mothers and infants, while those associated non-nucleosides or major PIs were not.
transmission of resistance is not consistent for all mutations and is not necessarily concordant between mother and infant.
we can use the information from the mother’s virus and the infant’s virus to help guide therapy for the infant, especially if the infant is not yet symptomatic.
